name: External oblique
func: The largest and outermost flat muscle on the side of the belly. It bends and twists the trunk, holds the belly in, and squeezes the abdomen to help with coughing and breathing out hard.

levels.kid:
Put your hands in your front pockets. The way your fingers point, down and toward the middle, is the same way the muscle on the side of your belly runs! It is called the **external oblique**.

It is a big, flat muscle on each side of your tummy. It wraps around like a **belt**.

It helps you **twist** your body, **bend sideways**, and sit up from lying down. It also squeezes your tummy when you **cough**, sneeze or blow out birthday candles. It helps hold everything inside your belly snug and safe.
levels.hs:
The **external oblique** is the largest and most superficial of the three flat muscles of the side (anterolateral) abdominal wall. Beneath it lie the **internal oblique** and then the **transversus abdominis**. Its fibres run **downward and forward**, in the same direction as your fingers in your front pockets.

It starts with finger-like slips from the outer surfaces of the **lower eight ribs (5–12)**, which interlock with **serratus anterior** and latissimus dorsi. It inserts on the **iliac crest** of the hip bone and, in front, becomes a broad flat sheet of tendon called an **aponeurosis**. This aponeurosis joins the one from the other side at the **linea alba**, the midline seam down the middle of the belly.

The lower edge of the aponeurosis folds back on itself between the **anterior superior iliac spine** and the **pubic tubercle**, forming the **inguinal ligament**.

Actions: acting on both sides, it **flexes the trunk** (as in a sit-up) and **compresses the abdomen**, raising pressure inside it for coughing, forced breathing out and lifting. Acting on one side, it **bends the trunk sideways** and **rotates it to the opposite side**.

It is supplied by the **thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T11)** and the **subcostal nerve (T12)**.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** external surfaces of ribs 5–12; insertion into the anterior half of the iliac crest, the pubic tubercle and, via its aponeurosis, the linea alba. Its free posterior border, between the 12th rib and the iliac crest, forms one side of the **inferior lumbar (Petit's) triangle**, with latissimus dorsi and the iliac crest.

**Rectus sheath:** the external oblique aponeurosis passes **in front of** the rectus abdominis along its whole length, forming part of the anterior rectus sheath.

**Inguinal canal:** the aponeurosis forms the **anterior wall** of the inguinal canal. A triangular opening in it above the pubic tubercle is the **superficial inguinal ring**. The aponeurosis also contributes to the **lacunar ligament** and **pectineal ligament**, and its in-rolled lower border, the inguinal ligament, forms the floor of the canal and the roof over structures passing from the abdomen into the thigh (femoral nerve, artery and vein).

**Rotation partner:** the external oblique of one side works with the **internal oblique of the opposite side**, since their fibres line up in a continuous diagonal. Turning the trunk to the right uses the left external oblique and right internal oblique.

**Innervation:** ventral rami **T7–T11** (thoracoabdominal) and **T12** (subcostal), running between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis. The skin over it follows the same dermatomes: T10 at the umbilicus.

**Blood supply:** lower posterior intercostal and subcostal arteries, and branches of the superior and inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries.
levels.phd:
The layered, cross-ply arrangement of the three flat abdominal muscles is a mechanical design similar to plywood. Fibres of the external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis run at different angles, so together they resist stress in multiple directions while allowing the wall to stretch. Their aponeuroses show a lattice of collagen fibres that, in the linea alba, are arranged in multiple interwoven directions, giving it great strength across the midline.

The external oblique is a key part of the **trunk "corset"** that generates **intra-abdominal pressure (IAP)**. IAP stiffens the lumbar spine during lifting; together with the diaphragm and pelvic floor, the abdominal muscles act as a pressurised cylinder. Researchers still debate how much IAP directly unloads the spine versus simply stiffening it.

In **respiration**, quiet expiration is passive, but during forced expiration (coughing, exercise) the abdominal muscles contract. Recordings show the transversus abdominis and internal oblique are often recruited before the external oblique.

**Motor control** studies of low back pain (Hodges and colleagues) found delayed feedforward activation of deep abdominal muscles, especially transversus abdominis, in people with back pain, while superficial muscles like the external oblique sometimes show increased activity, a "bracing" strategy. These findings have influenced but not fully validated "core stability" training.

Developmentally, the abdominal wall muscles derive from the **hypaxial dermomyotome** of thoracic somites, migrating ventrally. Failures of body-wall closure lead to defects such as **gastroschisis** and **omphalocele**, while **prune belly syndrome** involves deficient abdominal wall muscles.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** inspect the abdominal wall for asymmetry and bulges when the patient lifts the head and shoulders off the bed (Carnett's sign: if tenderness persists or worsens with the muscles tensed, the pain is likely in the abdominal wall rather than inside). Test the **superficial abdominal reflexes** by stroking the skin toward the umbilicus; they are lost in upper motor neuron lesions. **Beevor's sign**, upward movement of the umbilicus on sitting up, suggests weakness of the lower abdominal muscles from a lesion around T10.

**Inguinal hernias:** because the external oblique aponeurosis forms the front wall of the inguinal canal, it is opened during open hernia repair. Direct hernias bulge through the posterior wall (Hesselbach's triangle), while indirect hernias pass through the deep ring and along the canal to exit at the superficial ring. The **ilioinguinal nerve**, lying just deep to the aponeurosis, must be protected to avoid chronic groin pain.

**Surgical incisions** cut, split or retract these muscles. A **McBurney (gridiron) incision** for appendicectomy splits the external oblique along its fibres. Segmental nerves run between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis, so long vertical lateral incisions can denervate muscle and cause bulging.

**Abdominal wall hernias** also occur through the inferior lumbar triangle (Petit's hernia) and along the linea semilunaris (**Spigelian hernia**). **Rectus sheath haematoma** and side strains of the oblique muscles in athletes cause localised pain. Ultrasound and CT are the main imaging tests.

**Diastasis recti**, a widening of the linea alba, is distinct from a true hernia because there is no fascial defect.

keyPoints: Outermost and largest flat abdominal muscle; fibres run 'hands in pockets'
From ribs 5–12 to the iliac crest and linea alba
Its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament and the canal's front wall
Flexes, side-bends and rotates the trunk to the opposite side

test.q: Which way do the fibres of the external oblique run?
The in-rolled lower edge of the external oblique aponeurosis is the ______ ligament.
test.explain: It runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle.

test.q: Contracting the left external oblique rotates the trunk toward which side?
test.explain: The external oblique rotates the trunk to the opposite side, working with the opposite internal oblique.

test.q: Which nerves supply the external oblique?
test.explain: Thoracoabdominal nerves T7–T11 and the subcostal nerve T12.

test.q: The midline seam where left and right aponeuroses meet is the linea ______.
test.explain: Latin for 'white line', made of interwoven aponeurotic fibres.
